variant. Every op that produces a result either propagates the
tag or strips it. Built-ins gain tag-aware versions.

- Expensive: every existing op needs to handle the new variant,
  every demo needs to check what gets stripped, the tag
  propagation rules are non-trivial (does `W1 + W2` produce a
  `Weight` or just an array?).
- Powerful: anonymous intermediates retain their identity. The
  loss `mean((apply(mdl, X) - Y) * (...))` could be tagged
  `Loss { kind: MSE }` automatically.
- Probably too much work for v0.7.x. Reserve for after Saga 11.5.

**Recommendation:** start with Path 1 (side table). It is
additive, contained to `mlpl-eval`, and unblocks the `:describe`
improvements that motivate this proposal. Path 2 is the sequel.

## Typing-assistance loop for users (and agents)

The point of all this is to enable a *conversation* between the
user and the workspace:

    mlpl> mdl = chain(linear(2, 8, 11), tanh_layer(), linear(8, 2, 12))
    mlpl> :describe mdl
    mdl -- chain(2 hidden layers, 1 output layer)
      input:  shape [n, 2]
      output: shape [n, 2]
      hidden activations: 1 (after linear_1, kind=tanh)
      params: 4 -- W1[2,8], b1[1,8], W2[8,2], b2[1,2]
    mlpl> :describe W1
    W1 -- Weight (layer: mdl.linear_0)
      shape: [in=2, out=8]
      role:  trainable parameter
      grad:  computed at last adam() call (step 47)
    mlpl> :hidden mdl 0     ; brand-new command
    [Activation tanh, layer mdl.linear_0]
    shape: [n, 8]
    last computed at step 47

Every line of that session is unblocked by tagging. None of it
is unblocked by the language as it stands today.

Agents benefit even more. A tagged value gives an LLM a
concrete schema to follow when constructing or repairing a
program: "I need a `Weight` of shape `[in, out]` to plug into
this `Linear` layer", instead of "I need an array, hopefully of
the right shape, hopefully not a bias, hopefully not a
gradient".

## Open questions

- **Tag propagation for anonymous values.** Tier-A side-table
  tags only attach to bindings. Do we want to add a
  "register on assign" rule so that `g = grad(loss, W1)` is
  automatically tagged `Gradient { wrt: W1 }`? Probably yes.
  How far does it go?
- **Subtyping.** Is a `Weight` also an `Array`? Yes -- ops that
  take an array should accept a tagged value transparently. The
  reverse is not true: a built-in that demands a `Weight` should
  refuse a plain array.
- **Mutation.** When `W1 = W1 - lr * grad(...)`, does the tag
  carry through the assignment? Yes if the rhs is "obviously" a
  weight update (Path 2 territory). With a side table, tags are
  per-name and survive reassignment by default.
- **User-defined tags.** Should users be able to define their
  own roles? `tag(x, "MyMemoryRow")`? Yes eventually, but
  probably not in the first step. Start with the curated Tier A
  vocabulary.
- **Interaction with named axes.** A `Weight` *and* labeled axes
  are complementary: the role says "this is a trainable weight
  matrix", the labels say "axis 0 is `in_features`, axis 1 is
  `out_features`". They compose without conflict.
- **Models as parameter trees.** `:describe mdl` should walk the
  ModelSpec and pretty-print each layer with its inferred input
  and output shapes. This is achievable today (even before
  tags) and could be a small follow-up.

## Suggested first-step deliverable

Something small and concrete to validate the approach before
committing to a full saga:

> Add a `ValueTag` enum with the Tier-A variants, a
> `tags: HashMap<String, ValueTag>` side table on `Environment`,
> a `:describe` rendering that consumes the tag, and a
> `:tag <name> <kind>` REPL command for manually attaching a
> tag. Wire `linear()` and friends to auto-tag the params they
> create as `Weight` / `Bias`, and `grad()` to auto-tag its
> result as `Gradient { wrt }`. No new built-ins beyond `:tag`,
> no parser changes, no new `Value` variant. One commit, one
> step, fully reversible.

If that lands cleanly and the `:describe` output proves useful
in practice, the next step is the same treatment for `Loss`,
`LearningRate`, `Labels`, and `Activation`. Then iterate.

## Saga shaping

This is at least one full saga's worth of work, possibly two:

- **Saga 11.7 -- Typed ML concepts (Tier A):** `ValueTag`
  enum, side table, `:tag` / `:untag` REPL commands,
  auto-tagging from `linear()` / `chain()` / `grad()` / `adam()`
  / `cosine_schedule()`, expanded `:describe` output for tagged
  values, tutorial lesson "Typed ML Concepts", regression
  tests. ~6-8 steps.
- **Saga 11.8 -- Typed ML concepts (Tier B):** `Layer` /
  `Optimizer` / `Schedule` / `Dataset` roles, layer-aware
  `:describe mdl` walker that prints the model as a typed tree,
  contract checks at op boundaries (e.g. "loss expression for
  `adam` must be a `Loss`-tagged scalar"). ~6-8 steps.

Tier C overlaps with the paper-driven backlog and should be
folded into the relevant feature sagas (memory in 18, skills
and tools in 18, etc.) rather than a single typing saga.

## See also

- `docs/typing.md` -- the *current* typing model (untyped
  homogeneous arrays).
- `docs/milestone-named-axes.md` -- Saga 11.5, which adds
  labeled axes (compatible and complementary).
- `docs/are-we-driven-yet.md` -- the audit that surfaced the
  gap between the agent-driven wishlist and what MLPL has today.
- `docs/paper-driven-development.txt` -- the paper backlog that
  most Tier C concepts will land alongside.

# MLPL Multi-Saga Plan

This plan sequences the remaining work from `docs/research2.txt`
(the small-LLM / training-platform vision) against the current
state of the repo. Completed sagas are listed in `docs/saga.md`;
through v0.4 we have the language core, REPL, SVG viz, ML
built-ins, and six end-to-end demos, but every demo still carries
its own hand-written gradients. Everything downstream of autograd
depends on removing that limitation.

## Guiding principles

- Each saga delivers a visible user-facing win (a demo or a
  workflow), not just plumbing.
- Preserve the "thinking space" loop: train -> visualize ->
  adjust. Visualization is core syntax, not an afterthought.
- Backends (MLX, CUDA) come only after the CPU path is correct,
  tested, and expressive enough to be worth accelerating.
- Keep the cellular crate layout; new capabilities land as new
  crates, not as bulges in existing ones.
- TDD + quality gates per CLAUDE.md on every step.

## Completed sagas (context)

- **Saga -1** Repo scaffolding
- **Saga 0** Foundation and contracts
- **Saga 1** Dense tensor substrate v1 (Shape, DenseArray, reshape, transpose, indexing)
- **Saga 2** Parser and evaluator foundation
- **Saga 3** CLI and REPL v1
- **Saga 4** Structured trace v1 (JSON export)
- **Saga 5** Visual web viewer v1 -- DEFERRED
- **Saga 6** ML foundations (v0.2): sigmoid, tanh, pow, comparisons,
  axis reductions, mean, zeros/ones/fill, logistic regression demo
- **Saga 7** SVG visualization v1 (v0.3): `mlpl-viz`, `svg()`,
  scatter/line/bar/heatmap/decision_boundary, hist, scatter_labeled,
  loss_curve, confusion_matrix, boundary_2d, browser REPL inline SVG
- **Saga 8** ML demos (v0.4): random/randn/argmax/blobs/softmax/one_hot;
  k-means, PCA, softmax classifier, tiny MLP, attention pattern demos;
  tutorial lessons for each
- **Saga 9** Autograd v1 (v0.5): `mlpl-autograd` reverse-mode tape;
  `param[...]` / `tensor[...]` constructors; `grad(expr, wrt)` built-in;
  tiny MLP and softmax classifier demos ported off hand-written backprop;
  "Automatic differentiation" tutorial lesson
- **Saga 10** Optimizers + training loop (v0.6): `momentum_sgd` and
  `adam` built-ins with per-param state on the environment;
  `cosine_schedule` / `linear_warmup` scalar helpers; `moons` and
  `circles` synthetic datasets; new `train N { body }` construct
  with implicit `step` binding and `last_losses` capture;
  `moons_mlp` and `circles_mlp` demos; "Optimizers and Schedules"
  tutorial lesson
- **Saga 11.5** Named axes and shape introspection (v0.7.5):
  `LabeledShape` on `mlpl-core`; `label` / `relabel` /
  `reshape_labeled` builtins; `x : [batch, dim] = ...` annotation
  syntax; label propagation through elementwise, matmul,
  reduce/argmax, and `map()`; axis-name arg for
  `reduce_add`/`reduce_mul`/`argmax`/`softmax`; structured
  `EvalError::ShapeMismatch` with op-aware Display; label-aware
  `:vars`/`:describe` and trace JSON; "Named Axes" tutorial
  lesson and labeled Model Composition example
- **Compile-to-Rust saga** (v0.8.0): `mlpl-rt` runtime target,
  `mlpl-lower-rs` AST -> `TokenStream` codegen (scalar, array,
  fncall, variable, labels, matmul with static contraction
  check), `mlpl-macro` proc-macro, `mlpl` facade crate with
  hidden `__rt` re-export, `mlpl-build` CLI that compiles a
  `.mlpl` file to a native binary (and cross-compiles to
  wasm32-unknown-unknown), `mlpl-parity-tests` harness proving
  bit-for-bit agreement on 9 programs. Measured 9.05x speedup
  on a 100x100 reshape+reduce workload. See
  `docs/milestone-compile-to-rust.md`.
- **Saga 12** Tokenizers, datasets, experiment tracking
  (v0.9.0): `load`/`load_preloaded` with `--data-dir` sandbox;
  `shuffle`/`batch`/`batch_mask`/`split`/`val_split` dataset
  prep; `for row in ds { body }` streaming iteration;
  byte-level tokenizer (`tokenize_bytes`/`decode_bytes`);
  `Value::Tokenizer` + `TokenizerSpec::{ByteLevel,BpeMerges}`
  with `train_bpe`/`apply_tokenizer`/`decode`; `experiment
  "name" { body }` with `_metric` capture and `ExperimentRecord`
  logged to memory + `--exp-dir/<name>/<ts>/run.json`;
  `:experiments` + `compare(a, b)` registry; UTF-8 string-
  literal fix in the lexer; string-valued variable bindings.
  Three new tutorial lessons. See `docs/milestone-tokenizers.md`.
- **Saga 11** Model DSL (v0.7): `Value::Model` runtime value;
  `linear(in, out, seed)` atomic layer; parameter-free
  `tanh_layer` / `relu_layer` / `softmax_layer` activations;
  `chain(...)` sequential composition; `residual(block)` skip
  connections; `rms_norm(dim)` normalization; `attention(
  d_model, heads, seed)` multi-head self-attention (tape-lowered
  for `heads=1`); `params(model)` walker and optimizer
  integration so `adam(loss, mdl, ...)` walks the parameter
  tree; differentiable `apply(mdl, X)`; `moons_mlp` and
  `tiny_mlp` demos ported to one-line `chain(...)` form; new
  `transformer_block.mlpl` demo (loss 143.87 -> 1.02 over 100
  Adam steps); `:vars` / `:models` / `:fns` / `:wsid` /
  `:describe` REPL introspection commands; "Model Composition"
  tutorial lesson. See `docs/milestone-modeldsl.md`.

## Future saga sequence

### Saga 11.5 -- Named axes and shape introspection (COMPLETE, v0.7.5)
Shipped: `LabeledShape` type on `mlpl-core`; `label(x, [...])` /
`relabel(x, [...])` / `reshape_labeled(x, dims, labels)` builtins;
`x : [batch, time, dim] = ...` annotation syntax; label propagation
through elementwise (with `merge_labels`), matmul (contraction
axis validated, outer dims threaded), reduce/argmax (reduced
axis's label dropped), and `map()` (preserves through math
builtins); axis-name arg for `reduce_add` / `reduce_mul` /
`argmax` / `softmax`; structured `EvalError::ShapeMismatch { op,
expected, actual }` with op-aware Display; labels in `:vars` /
`:describe` (via `LabeledShape` Display) and in the trace JSON
export (serde-skip-when-None); "Named Axes" tutorial lesson and
labeled `apply(mdl, X)` in the Model Composition lesson.
Deferred: per-layer input/output label pinning on `:describe
<model>` (needs `Environment` signature tracking on first
`apply` -- a natural follow-up).

### Compile-to-Rust saga (COMPLETE, v0.8.0)
Shipped: `mlpl-rt` runtime target, `mlpl-lower-rs` (path-
configurable AST -> Rust TokenStream codegen), `mlpl-macro`
proc-macro (`mlpl! { ... }` emits `compile_error!` on lower
failure), `mlpl` facade crate, `mlpl-build` CLI
(`mlpl-build foo.mlpl -o foo [--target <triple>]`),
`mlpl-parity-tests` harness. Static matmul contraction check
at lower time; runtime label checks still catch anything the
static pass cannot resolve. 9.05x measured speedup on a 100x100
reshape+reduce workload. Deferred: `TensorCtor`, `Repeat`,
`Train`, autograd, optimizers, Model DSL -- they need tape-
state or loop lowering and sit in a follow-up.

### Saga 12 -- Tokenizers, datasets, and experiment tracking (COMPLETE, v0.9.0)
Shipped: `load`/`load_preloaded` with terminal-REPL
`--data-dir` sandbox and compiled-in web corpus registry;
dataset prep (`shuffle`, `batch`, `batch_mask`, `split`,
`val_split`); `for row in ds { body }` streaming iteration
with `last_rows` capture; byte-level BPE
(`tokenize_bytes`/`decode_bytes` primitives;
`Value::Tokenizer` + `TokenizerSpec::{ByteLevel,BpeMerges}`;
`train_bpe`/`apply_tokenizer`/`decode` with byte-lossless
round-trip); experiment tracking
(`experiment "name" { body }`, `_metric`-capture,
`ExperimentRecord` to `env.experiment_log` + optional
on-disk `<exp_dir>/<name>/<ts>/run.json`, `:experiments`
merge + `compare(a, b)` with per-metric deltas);
byproduct UTF-8 string-literal lexer fix; string-valued
variable bindings; three new tutorial lessons. Deferred:
`experiment` source-text capture (needs source threading
through eval), `load` sandbox disallowing absolute-path
canonicalized symlinks (currently path-component-based).

### Saga 13 -- Tiny LM end-to-end (NEXT)
Train a character-level or tiny-BPE language model (~1-5M params)
on a small corpus entirely in MLPL on CPU. Visualize loss,
sample generations, and attention maps. This is the first saga
that proves the platform thesis end-to-end.

### Saga 14 -- MLX backend (COMPLETE, v0.11.0)
Ten steps across five phases. Shipped: `crates/mlpl-mlx` runtime
target with matmul/elementwise/activations/reshape/transpose/
reductions/softmax/log_softmax/cross_entropy each parity-tested
vs CPU within fp32 tolerance; `device("mlx") { body }` scoped
form + `to_device(x, target)` movement helper + typed
`EvalError::DeviceMismatch`; Model DSL dispatch so `apply(model,
X)` inside an MLX block routes every matmul/softmax/add through
`mlpl-mlx`; autograd via tape re-materialization (grad matches
CPU within 1e-4 across every tape primitive); Adam/momentum_sgd/
`train N { }`/`experiment` all inherit; `demos/tiny_lm_mlx.mlpl`
training end-to-end with loss curve matching CPU; Criterion
bench harness (`mlpl-bench --features mlx`). Performance: 0.84x
reshape+reduce, 0.26x tiny_lm_train_step -- below the 5x gate;
bottlenecks diagnosed in `docs/benchmarks.md` (f32/f64
round-trip per op, no graph fusion, tape re-materialization,
small inner dims). Correctness intact. CUDA still Saga 17. See
`docs/milestone-mlx-backend.md`, `docs/using-mlx.md`
retrospective, and `docs/saga.md` Saga 14 entry.

### Saga 15 -- LoRA / QLoRA and quantization
`lora[rank=8] model`, layer-scoped adapters, shared subspaces,
4-bit quantization for the frozen base. Fine-tune the Saga 13
model on a small instruction set.

### Saga 16 -- Embedding visualization and RAG
`embed`, `plot pca/tsne/umap`, 3D scatter via SVG projection,
nearest-neighbor links. RAG pipeline demo over a small corpus.
Builds directly on the existing viz stack.

### Saga 17 -- CUDA backend and distributed execution (SUPERSEDED)
**Superseded** by the services refactor proposed in
`docs/refactor-services.md`. The original Saga 17 plan
was an in-process CUDA crate paralleling Saga 14's
in-process MLX crate; that approach has hardware
coupling problems (one binary can't link both MLX
and CUDA) and disk pressure problems (target/ tree
balloons further). The replacement plan:

- **Saga R1** -- refactor `mlpl-mlx` into
  `mlpl-mlx-serve` (a separate service binary
  reusing Saga 21's REST + auth machinery).
  Orchestrator gains peer routing for `device("mlx")
  { ... }` blocks. In-process MLX feature stays as
  a fallback. Disk benefit: separate target tree.
- **Saga R2** -- CUDA-as-a-service. Replaces
  Saga 17's in-process CUDA crate with
  `mlpl-cuda-serve` of the same shape as
  `mlpl-mlx-serve`. The Linux + NVIDIA dev host
  builds + tests it; the orchestrator + MLX peer
  can stay on the Mac.
- **Saga R3** -- distributed primitives (`run
  model on nodes[...]`, data-parallel training)
  layered on R1 + R2. Auto-discovery (mDNS) of
  peers on a LAN. The original "Saga 17
  distributed" content, just renumbered + layered
  on the service architecture.

See `docs/refactor-services.md` for the full
design + worked example + tensor lifecycle +
non-goals + open questions.

### Saga 18 -- Distillation, ICL/ICRL, engram memory
Distillation pipelines, trajectory-based updates, engram-style
memory attachments, and multi-model orchestration
(`orchestrate[planner, executor, verifier]`). The research
frontier items from section 6 of `research2.txt`.

### Saga 19 -- LLM-as-tool integration
REST client built-ins, teacher-model distillation workflows,
codegen helpers. Intentionally last in the "core platform"
sequence: secondary to the "build your own model" story.

### Saga 20 -- Perturbation research demos
Express the [Neural Thickets / nt-rs](https://github.com/swcraig/nt-rs)
algorithm (RandOpt-style weight perturbation specialists +
top-K ensembling) as a single MLPL program with a
specialization heatmap output. Adds four small builtins to the
language surface: `clone_model(m)` (deep copy with fresh param
names), `perturb_params(m, family, sigma, seed)` (family-targeted
randn add, where `family` matches the layer-name patterns the
Saga 11/13 model constructors already use internally),
`argtop_k(values, k)` (index-returning companion to the existing
`top_k`), and `scatter(buffer, index, value)` (scalar write into
a rank-1 array, sized to drive `repeat N` accumulation loops).
Headline demo `demos/neural_thicket.mlpl` trains a Saga 13 Tiny
LM as the base, sweeps four perturbation families on MLX, scores
on held-out tokens, runs a top-K ensemble, and renders a
`[family x seed]` heatmap. Stays single-process (no distributed
coordination -- that is Saga 17) and stays on the Tiny LM (no
real pretrained model -- that needs Saga 15+'s checkpoint format
or Saga 19's REST sidecar). Depends on Saga 14 for the variant-
loop speed budget. See `docs/mlpl-for-neural-thickets.md` for
the design sketch and full strawman source.

### Saga 21 -- CLI server + multi-client UI
New `crates/mlpl-serve` binary that exposes a REST + WebSocket
surface over a long-running MLPL interpreter. One server, many
clients: today's web UI wired to call origin (unblocks `:ask`
via a server-side Ollama reverse proxy -- no CORS gymnastics
on the client), `mlpl-repl --connect <host>`, an eventual
ratatui TUI, and an Emacs client that renders SVG in-buffer
without a browser. Session isolation per bearer token;
`--bind 0.0.0.0` requires `--auth required`; proxy allow-list
gates which LLM providers are reachable and server-side env
vars hold their keys. Ships with the CLI visualization
strategy (auto-write SVG to cache dir + print path) so the
terminal REPL stops dumping raw `<svg>` XML. MVP scope: new
crate skeleton, `POST /v1/sessions` + `POST /v1/.../eval`,
`mlpl-repl --connect`. After MVP: visualization storage +
URLs, proxy endpoints, streaming eval via SSE, cancellation.
Desktop GUI wrapper (tauri/wry) and Emacs client land in
follow-up sagas once the server surface is stable. See
`docs/configurations.md` for the configuration matrix, the
CLI-server architecture diagram, the REST API sketch, and the
security posture.

### Saga 22 -- Feasibility checking + resource estimation
Users on limited hardware (laptops, older GPUs) need a way
to sanity-check a planned operation BEFORE running it so
they don't hit OOM, fill disk, or discover a run will take
days. Saga 22 ships four builtins on top of the Model DSL
that answer "will this fit / how long will it take?"
without the user needing to commit to the run.
`estimate_train(model, steps, batch_size, seq_len [,
dtype_bytes]) -> [params, vram_bytes, disk_bytes, flops,
wall_seconds]` is pure-math over the ModelSpec tree:
walks `ModelSpec::params()`, sums parameter counts,
computes VRAM (fwd + grad + Adam moments + activation
heuristic), derives FLOPS per step by node type (Linear,
LinearLora, Embedding, Attention), and divides by a
device-throughput number to get wall-clock.
`calibrate_device() -> gflops` runs a canned 1024x1024
matmul benchmark on the active device, caches the observed
GFLOPS in `env` (CPU vs MLX cached separately), and makes
subsequent `estimate_train` calls honest instead of the
default conservative 50-GFLOPS lower bound.
`hypothetical_model(name) -> ModelSpec` returns a
structural ModelSpec for SmolLM-135M / 360M / 1.7B,
Llama-3.2-1B, Qwen2.5-0.5B so users can ask "how big would
a SmolLM-135M + LoRA(rank=8) fine-tune be on my laptop?"
WITHOUT needing to download the weights first. `apply` on
a hypothetical errors helpfully -- it is an estimation-only
spec. `feasible(estimate_result, [vram_budget, disk_budget,
wall_budget]) -> 0/1` is the guard pattern:
`if feasible(est, [4e9, 10e9, 600]) { train ... }`.
Zeros in the budget mean skip that dimension. Non-goals
(deferred): actual HuggingFace download + safetensors
parsing (separate future saga); f16/bf16 tensor
dtype machinery (what-if only today via `dtype_bytes`
argument); dynamic profiling (the estimator is honest-
approximate at ~2x accuracy); distributed / multi-GPU
estimation (Saga 17); automatic shrinking / recovery
(estimator reports, does not rewrite). CLI-first;
estimator itself works in web but `calibrate_device`
needs CLI. Depends on Saga 11 (Model DSL) + Saga 15
(LoRA freeze set).

## Dependency graph (abbreviated)

```
9 autograd
  |-- 10 optimizers -- 11 model DSL -- 11.5 named axes -- 12 data+tracking -- 13 tiny LM
  |                                                                                |
  |                                                                                +-- 14 MLX
  |                                                                                |    \-- 20 perturbation demos
  |                                                                                +-- 15 LoRA
  |                                                                                +-- 16 viz/RAG
  |                                                                                +-- 17 SUPERSEDED -> R1/R2/R3 (services refactor; see docs/refactor-services.md)
  |                                                                                +-- 18 distill/ICRL
  |                                                                                +-- 21 CLI server
  |                                                                                +-- 19 LLM REST
  |                                                                                +-- 22 feasibility/estimation (also uses 15)
```

Sagas 14-19 + 22 can reorder based on hardware access and
interest; 9-13 (plus the inserted 11.5) must run in order.
Saga 20 needs 14 finished (variant-loop throughput) but is
otherwise free to slot wherever a research-demo cycle makes
sense. Saga 22 was queued ahead of Saga 19 because the
feasibility checker landed value for every existing user
immediately; it shipped as v0.15.0 on 2026-04-24. Saga 19
followed and shipped as v0.16.0 on 2026-04-24. Saga 21
(CLI server) is next, prioritized ahead of the Linux
host move so the live browser demo keeps working without
local MLX once dev moves off Apple Silicon.

## Start next: Saga R1 -- mlpl-mlx as a service (services refactor)

Saga 21 (v0.17.0) just shipped the MVP CLI server +
`mlpl-repl --connect` client + CLI viz cache. The
next high-leverage move is **the services refactor**
proposed in `docs/refactor-services.md`: promote
`mlpl-mlx` from an in-process Cargo feature to a
standalone service binary (`mlpl-mlx-serve`) that
the orchestrator dispatches `device("mlx") { ... }`
blocks to. This unlocks three things at once:

1. **Cross-host MLX from a Linux dev host.** Run
   the orchestrator on Linux; MLX peer on the Mac;
   `device("mlx") { train ... }` blocks ship as
   program source, run on the Mac, return handles.
2. **Hardware coupling escape** for Saga R2
   (CUDA-as-a-service, replacing the deferred
   in-process Saga 17). One binary still can't
   link both MLX and CUDA, but one orchestrator
   can route to peers that each link one.
3. **Disk pressure relief.** `mlpl-mlx-serve` lives
   in its own service workspace with its own
   `target/`. The main workspace's `target/` no
   longer compiles the MLX bindings.

R1 keeps the in-process MLX feature as a fallback
so existing single-host MLX users don't regress;
the new "remote MLX peer" path is additive. R2
follows once R1's protocol is settled. R3 layers
distributed primitives + auto-discovery on top.

The planned saga decomposition lives in
`docs/refactor-services.md`. Open questions to
resolve before R1 begins: peer-to-peer auth
beyond loopback, tensor wire-format choice,
strict-fault vs auto-fetch on cross-device ops,
streaming for long-running blocks. None of these
gate the design itself, but they shape R1's first
contract.

aiTitle: Analyze project status and identify missing sagas

content.text:
## Status snapshot

You're at v0.18.0, with Sagas through 22 + R1 shipped. From research3.txt's wishlist, you already have:

- **Tensor / Shape / Axis** → `DenseArray` + `LabeledShape` (Saga 11.5)
- **Layer / Parameter** → `Value::Model` + `ModelSpec` (Saga 11)
- **Gradient** → `grad()` + tape (Saga 9)
- **OptimizerState / Schedule** → adam/momentum_sgd + cosine/warmup (Saga 10)
- **Loss ops** → `cross_entropy`, MSE composition (Sagas 9, 13)
- **Attention building blocks** → `attention`, `causal_attention`, `attention_weights` (Sagas 11, 13)
- **Dataset / Transform** → `load`, `batch`, `shuffle`, `split`, `for row in ds` (Saga 12)
- **Embedding / table introspection** → `embed`, `embed_table` (Sagas 13, 16.5)

Crucially, all of these are **values, not typed concepts**. There's no language-level distinction between a `Logit` and a `Probability`, no first-class `Distribution`, no inspectable `ComputationGraph`. `docs/typed-ml-concepts.md` already proposed Tier A/B/C tags but was never sequenced into the plan.

## Proposed sagas (in dependency order)

### Saga 23 — Typed ML values (Tier A) — *highest leverage*
Ship `docs/typed-ml-concepts.md` Tier A as the foundation everything else builds on: `Logit`, `Probability`, `Loss`, `Gradient`, `Weight`, `Bias`, `Activation`, `LearningRate`, `Labels` as `ValueTag`s on Environment side-table. Auto-tag from `softmax`/`grad`/`linear`/`cross_entropy`. Critical win: `softmax` upgrades a `Logit` → `Probability`, and `cross_entropy(probs, _)` errors with "expected Logit, got Probability" — catches the most common ML bug. Path 1 (side table) per the design doc.

### Saga 24 — Distributions as first-class values
Add `Distribution` value variant with `Categorical`, `Gaussian`, `Mixture` constructors. Operations: `sample(dist, seed)`, `log_prob(dist, x)`, `entropy(dist)`, `kl_divergence(p, q)`. Ties into typed `Probability` from Saga 23. Unlocks variational/generative demos (VAE, mixture density nets) and gives `:describe` something rich to render.

### Saga 25 — Inspectable computation graph (`ComputationGraph` / `Tape` as a value)
Today the autograd tape is internal to `mlpl-autograd`. Surface it as `Value::Graph` with `forward_pass(graph)`, `backward_pass(graph)`, `nodes(graph)`, `edges(graph)`, plus a new `svg(graph, "compute_graph")` viz type. Pairs with `animate(graph)` for the "value → operation → shape change → gradient consequence" loop research3.txt calls out as the organizing principle. Also unlocks `jacobian(f, x)` and `hessian(f, x)` as derived ops.

### Saga 26 — Typed Layer interfaces (Tier B)
After Tier A bakes in, lift `ModelSpec` variants to typed roles: `Layer { input_kind, output_kind, params }`, `ActivationLayer`, plus per-layer input/output label pinning on `:describe mdl` (already flagged as a deferred follow-up to Saga 11.5). Enables `:hidden mdl 0` to return a tagged `Activation` value and `:describe` to walk the model as a typed tree. Most of the design is already in `typed-ml-concepts.md` §Tier B.

### Saga 27 — Sinkhorn + normalization family
research3.txt explicitly calls out `sinkhorn_normalize` as a missing core op alongside the layer/batch/RMS norms you already have. Add `sinkhorn_normalize`, `temperature_scale`, plus the missing loss family: `kl_divergence`, `contrastive_loss`, `triplet_loss`. Small saga, but completes the operation matrix and gives optimal-transport demos something to stand on.

### Saga 28 — Animated transform visualization
`animate(value_before, op, value_after)` and `explain_transform(op)` from research3.txt §5. Builds on Saga 25's graph value: render a sequence of SVG frames showing shape change + gradient flow as an op runs. Requires Saga 7's viz stack and the Saga 25 graph. The "thinking space" payoff your project README leans on.

### Saga 29 — Typed Dataset / Sample / Feature / Label
Tier B finish: turn the tuple-of-arrays Dataset shape into a `Dataset` role with `inputs`, `labels`, `n_classes`, plus `Sample`/`Feature`/`Transform` tags so `confusion_matrix(preds, labels)` can validate matching class counts at the language level rather than at the renderer.

## Recommended ordering & main tradeoff

**23 → 24 → 25 → 26 → 27 → 28 → 29.** Saga 23 is the keystone — every other saga in this list reads cleaner once tags exist. The tradeoff: pinning typed-ML semantics into the language now means more invariants for future sagas (R2 CUDA, 18 distillation) to preserve. If you'd rather keep the language permissive and ship more capabilities first, swap 23 to last and treat it as a polish saga. My read is the opposite: research3.txt is essentially asking you to make the language's ML concepts *visible*, which **is** the typing work.

Want me to draft a full milestone doc for Saga 23 (`docs/milestone-typed-values.md`) along the lines of the existing milestone-* files, so it's ready to seed an agentrail plan?

> no dtype, no static type checking, and no first-class function
> type.

no first-class functions.

- Booleans from `gt` / `lt` / `eq` are the floats `0.0` and `1.0`.

  are checked at the call boundary by demanding a scalar with
  zero fractional part, then stored as `f64` like everything else.

  weights are all out of scope until a future saga adds dtype.

  `EvalError::Unsupported(..)`.

  incompatible array shapes.
- Reductions check the axis index is in bounds.

no shape inference, no shape-polymorphic compilation, no

optional annotation `x : [batch, time, dim] = ...` but that

- You cannot pass a model as an argument to another model.
- You cannot store models in an array.
- You cannot return a model from a built-in or from a `repeat`
  body (the `repeat` body returns a scalar).
- You cannot generalize over a model's arity -- every model takes
  exactly one rank-2 tensor input and returns one rank-2 tensor.

|-----------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **MLPL v0.7.0** | dynamic, untyped, single homogeneous `f64` buffer, runtime shape checks       |

| BQN             | dynamic, untyped, with array-of-array nesting and first-class functions       |

  will run until it can't.
- That the dtype of a value is preserved across an op. There is

content.text:
## What "type" means in MLPL today

It's almost nothing. From `docs/typing.md`: every binding holds one of three variants — `Array` (a `DenseArray` of `f64`), `Model` (a `ModelSpec` tree), or `Str`. That's the *entire* type universe. There's no dtype (everything's `f64`), no integer/float distinction, no tuples, no nullables, no first-class functions, no record types.

What you actually have is **shape as structural metadata** that ops check on entry. `matmul` rejects when the contraction dim doesn't agree. Saga 11.5 promoted this with `LabeledShape` — axis names threaded through ops — but those are explicitly *metadata, not types*. The Saga 14 `device("mlx")` tag and the R1 `DeviceTensor` handle are de-facto types too, but again only enforced at op entry. It's all dynamic, all op-local, all "the first call that fails is the one that crashes."

So the answer is: **a "type" in MLPL today is a runtime-checked predicate that some operation chose to enforce.** There is no type *system* — just a scattered collection of guards.

## What it could become

There are at least five orthogonal axes, and you have to decide which ones you commit to:

| Axis | What it tracks | MLPL today | Cost to add |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Dtype** | f32 / f16 / bf16 / i32 / bool | f64 only | high (every op needs dispatch) |
| **Structural** | rank + dim sizes + (optionally) axis labels | shape via LabeledShape | already paid; needs surfacing |
| **Semantic** | Logit vs Probability vs Loss vs Weight | nothing | medium (tag side-table) |
| **Algebraic** | Distribution = Categorical \| Gaussian \| Mixture | implicit in `Value` enum | medium (variant + dispatch) |
| **Effectful** | on-device, on-tape, frozen, requires-grad | device tag, frozen set | already exists, not unified |

Several of these you've already built — they just aren't *called* types. Promoting them to types means: (a) giving names to the predicates, (b) surfacing them in `:describe`, (c) checking earlier than op-entry, and (d) letting users *write* them in source.

## Are you a candidate for optional / gradual types? Yes — strongly.

The APL family splits cleanly here:

- **APL2 / J / BQN**: deliberately untyped. Rank polymorphism is the whole product; types would smother it.
- **Futhark / Dex**: fully statically typed array languages with shape-polymorphic kinds.
- **MLPL**: sits at the untyped end *by inheritance*, not by design conviction.

What makes MLPL a good candidate for **optional** typing rather than mandatory typing:

1. **Every value already carries the data a type would describe** — shape, labels, device, frozen-status, and (for Models) a structural spec tree. You're not building a type system from scratch; you're naming what the runtime already tracks.
2. **The audience already thinks in shapes.** ML engineers write `# (B, T, D)` comments above every line. MLPL can promote that comment to a checked annotation.
3. **You have a static-compilation seam.** The `mlpl!` macro and `mlpl build` already emit `LowerError::StaticShapeMismatch → compile_error!` when both labels are known at lower time. Static type checks have a natural place to live without disturbing the dynamic REPL path.
4. **The language is still small enough to retrofit.** A type system bolted onto a 100k-LOC codebase is expensive. Bolted onto MLPL today it's a saga, not a rewrite.
5. **APL elegance and optional types coexist.** Rank polymorphism survives if you treat dim sizes as universally quantified by default and only check what's annotated. `softmax : Logit[*..., axis] → Probability[*..., axis]` is rank-polymorphic *and* type-safe.

The model that fits is **gradual typing** in the TypeScript / mypy / Sorbet sense: types are optional, inference fills gaps, and unannotated code keeps working unchanged. The runtime stays the source of truth; types are *additional* predicates checked when present.

## Practical implications

**If you add optional types** (the path I'd recommend):

- Wins:
  - The `Logit` vs `Probability` distinction catches the single most common ML bug at the call site of `cross_entropy`. This alone pays for the saga.
  - Shape mismatches surface before the 30-minute training run starts. Today they surface in step 3 of train, which means lost wall-clock and a confused-looking `:experiments` log.
  - `:describe` becomes a real interface — agents and humans both get a schema to reason against.
  - The compile-to-Rust path lifts more checks into `compile_error!` instead of runtime panics, expanding what `mlpl!` can guarantee.
  - Saga 22 feasibility checks become *type-driven*: `estimate_train` knows the input is a `ModelSpec`, not just hopes so.
- Costs:
  - Parser surface grows (annotation syntax beyond Saga 11.5's labels).
  - You must commit to inference. Nobody writes `x : Tensor[Batch=32, Token=128, Dim=768]` by hand on every line; if inference is weak, the system rots into ignored annotations.
  - You must define type-vs-runtime divergence rules. A `Probability` whose values sum to 1.0001 — type-valid, value-invalid? Pick a rule and document it.
  - Risk of half-building. A type system that rejects half of valid programs and accepts half of invalid ones is worse than no type system.

**If you don't add types**:

- Wins:
  - Language stays APL-small. REPL turn-around stays snappy. Demo code stays terse.
  - Rank polymorphism stays uncomplicated.
  - Less surface for agents and humans to learn.
- Costs:
  - The same shape bug ships in ten different demos with ten different error messages.
  - Every program carries type info *in comments*, which rot.
  - `cross_entropy(softmax(logits), Y)` — the textbook double-softmax bug — is silently a NaN factory rather than a compile error. This is exactly what research3.txt §1 calls out: "A Logit should not be silently treated as a probability."
  - Agent-driven workflows stay weak because LLMs need a schema to reason against, and "everything is an f64 array" is not a useful schema.

## Why not track type explicitly when every instance has shape/rank/value?

You should. The honest answer to your question is: **the runtime is already doing 80% of the work a type system would do**; promoting it just means giving the predicates names, surfacing them, and pushing the check earlier in the pipeline.

The deliberate-untyped position only makes sense for languages where rank polymorphism is the entire product (APL/J/BQN). MLPL is *not* that language — it's a typed-ML platform that happens to be APL-shaped. The Saga roadmap (estimate-then-train, named axes, freeze/unfreeze, device dispatch, model DSL) has been quietly building toward typed values from the start. The typing layer is the missing keystone.

## Concrete recommendation

A four-layer gradual-typing rollout, each layer independently shippable:

1. **Layer 0 — surface what exists.** Promote `Value` variant + shape + labels + device + frozen-status to a unified `:type x` REPL command and a `kind(x)` builtin. No new checks, no new annotations. Just naming. ~1 step.
2. **Layer 1 — semantic tags (the Saga 23 from my previous answer).** `Logit`, `Probability`, `Loss`, `Gradient`, `Weight`, `Bias`, `Activation` as side-table tags from `typed-ml-concepts.md` Tier A. Auto-tagged by the ops that produce them. Ops that consume them check the tag.
3. **Layer 2 — annotations as predicates.** Extend Saga 11.5's `x : [batch, time, dim] = ...` to accept type names: `x : Logit[batch, token]`. Annotation = a predicate the runtime asserts on assignment, like a `debug_assert` you can't turn off. Inference fills the unannotated case.
4. **Layer 3 — static checking on the compile-to-Rust path.** Whatever the runtime can check, the lowerer should try to check at lower time and emit `compile_error!`. The dynamic REPL path stays unchanged; the `mlpl!` and `mlpl build` paths get progressively stricter.

The crucial design move is keeping the layers **strictly additive**. A program with no annotations and no tags must still work exactly as it does today. The type system is a flashlight, not a fence.

Want me to write this up as `docs/optional-typing-design.md` so it can become the seed for a future saga, or sketch what the annotation syntax would look like concretely first?

## How each goal reshapes the typing decision

**Educational first** is the biggest reframe. It pushes typing toward being a *teaching surface*, not a correctness mechanism that happens to teach. Concretely:

- **Annotations should be encouraged, not just inferred.** TypeScript-style "let inference do everything" is correctness-first thinking. Educational-first wants the student to *write* `logits : Logit[batch, vocab]` because writing it is the lesson. Types become a vocabulary the student practices, not boilerplate the compiler hides.
- **Type names should be ML names, not language-theory names.** `Logit`, `Probability`, `AttentionMap`, `CrossEntropy` — not `T<f32, [N, V]>` or `Numeric<Phantom=Unnormalized>`. Names *are* pedagogy. A student who writes `softmax : Logit -> Probability` has learned something about softmax that no comment delivers.
- **Type errors should explain the ML mistake, not the type mismatch.** "Expected Logit, got Probability — `cross_entropy` expects raw scores, not a softmax output. If you already applied softmax, use `nll(probs, targets)` instead." That's a tutoring message wrapped around a type check.
- **`:describe` and trace JSON become curriculum.** Every traced event should show the typed transformation: `softmax: Logit[batch=4, vocab=8] -> Probability[batch=4, vocab=8]`. The trace is no longer a debug aid — it's a microscope on what each ML operation *does*.

**Correctness second** lines up with educational: the same predicates that teach also catch bugs. The double-softmax bug is the canonical example — it's both a learning moment and a real production hazard.

**Utility third** sets a ceiling on annotation cost. If writing types is too tedious, students give up and write untyped code, and the educational win evaporates. So annotations stay optional, and the runtime tags every value automatically. Untyped code still runs. Mixed code is normal.

**Practicality fourth** rules out parser-heavy machinery — no Hindley-Milner, no row polymorphism, no dependent types. Predicate-style runtime tags + light syntactic sugar is the practical ceiling.

**Maintainability fifth** argues for *one* mechanism — semantic tag — covering Logit/Probability/Loss/Weight/etc. Not three parallel systems (one for shapes, one for roles, one for distributions).

**Extensibility sixth** says users should eventually define their own tags (`tag(x, "MyMemoryRow")`) so research-grade concepts (Skill, Tool, Episode) don't need a language version bump. Tier C from `typed-ml-concepts.md` becomes user-defined, not core-defined.

**Performance last** is liberating. Every op can tag-check on entry. Every assignment can verify the predicate. Trace events can carry the full type. `:describe` can re-walk the model tree on every call. None of this needs to be free, because *none of it is on the performance frontier*.

## Refined recommendation

Drop the "Layer 3: static checking on the compile-to-Rust seam" from my previous answer. Static checking is a performance/correctness optimization — valuable, but lower-priority under your ranking. Keep the other three layers, and add an educational-first layer on top:

| Layer | Purpose | Goal served |
|---|---|---|
| 0. Surface what exists (`:type`, `kind()`) | Make today's runtime data visible | educational, correctness |
| 1. Semantic tags (Logit, Probability, Loss, ...) | Catch the ML-canonical bugs | educational, correctness |
| 2. Annotations as predicates (`x : Logit[batch, vocab]`) | Let students *write* the vocabulary | **educational** |
| **3. Typed traces + typed `:describe`** | Make every op a visible transformation | **educational** |
| 4. Tutoring error messages | Errors that teach the underlying ML concept | **educational** |
| 5. User-defined tags | Research-grade concepts without core changes | extensibility |
| 6. (Deferred) Static checks on `mlpl!` / `mlpl build` | Lift checks to compile time | correctness, performance |

Layer 3 is the addition your ranking forces. Right now, the trace JSON exports shape and value but no semantic meaning. Under educational-first, the trace should show `Logit[batch=4, vocab=8] --softmax--> Probability[batch=4, vocab=8]` for every step, so the web viewer (when it ships) can render the *transformation* graphically — exactly the "value_before -> operation -> value_after -> shape change" loop research3.txt §5 calls "the organizing principle."

## Saga sequence under this ranking

1. **Saga 23 (revised) — Typed ML values + typed traces.** Tier A tags from `typed-ml-concepts.md`, plus the trace and `:describe` upgrades. Ships the educational and correctness wins together. The trace upgrade is what makes this an *educational* saga rather than a *correctness* saga.
2. **Saga 24 — Distributions.** Distributions are pedagogically central to ML and missing from MLPL. `Categorical`, `Gaussian`, `Mixture` with `sample`, `log_prob`, `entropy`, `kl_divergence`. Builds on Saga 23's `Probability` tag.
3. **Saga 25 — Inspectable computation graph.** `ComputationGraph` / `ForwardPass` / `BackwardPass` as values, with `svg(graph, "compute_graph")` and `animate(graph)`. The visualization piece is what serves the educational goal — the static graph is just plumbing.
4. **Saga 26 — Annotation syntax + tutoring errors.** Extend Saga 11.5's `:` syntax to type names. Rewrite every type-related error message as a tutoring message. Sounds small; the error-message rewrite is the load-bearing educational work.
5. **Saga 27 — Typed Layer roles + walked `:describe mdl`.** Tier B from `typed-ml-concepts.md`. Per-layer input/output type and shape pinning so the model-tree printout becomes a teaching diagram.
6. **Saga 28 — User-defined tags.** `tag(x, "MyMemoryRow")`, `untag(x)`, `:tags` listing. Unlocks Tier C without core saga work for each concept.
7. **(Deferred) Static checks on the Rust seam.** Lifts a subset of Layer 1/2 checks to lower-time. Pure correctness/performance gain; ships when the dynamic story is solid.

The big shift from my last answer: **Saga 25 (computation graph) moves up the priority list** because its educational payoff is enormous (visible forward/backward flow), and **the compile-to-Rust static-check saga moves down** because it serves the goal you ranked last.

Want me to draft `docs/optional-typing-design.md` as the seed doc for Saga 23, with the educational-first framing baked in so the saga's success criteria are pedagogical (a student can read a trace and learn softmax) rather than just technical (no Logit-Probability mismatches)?

lastPrompt: Goals ranked: educational, correctness, utility, practicality, maintainability, extensibility, many others, then performance.

4	
5	`docs/are-we-driven-yet.md` flagged named-axes and shape-checking as
6	the single highest-leverage "agent usability" gap in the
7	`docs/ai-agent-driven-development.txt` wishlist. It is also the
8	common pain point behind half the shape errors you hit writing demos
9	by hand: once an expression has four matmul-reshape-transpose steps,
10	tracking which axis is which becomes the hard part.
11	
12	Positional indexing is opaque for both humans and agents:
13	
14	```mlpl
15	scores = matmul(Q, transpose(K)) / sqrt(4)   # which axis is which?
16	```
17	
18	Named indexing is self-documenting:
19	
20	```mlpl
21	Q : [seq, d_k]
22	K : [seq, d_k]
23	scores : [seq, seq] = matmul(Q, K.T["seq", "d_k" -> "d_k", "seq"])
24	```
25	
26	Saga 11.5 is a *surface-only* milestone: no new kernels, no new
27	backends, no new ML primitives. It teaches MLPL to carry axis labels
28	and shape metadata through the evaluator so error messages are
29	actionable and agents can reason about tensor validity before they
30	run code.
31	
32	This saga is inserted between Saga 11 (Model DSL) and Saga 12
33	(Tokenizers/datasets) because every later saga -- Tiny LM, LoRA,
34	attention variants, embedding viz -- benefits from labeled axes
35	and would otherwise accumulate the same hand-written shape-juggling
36	that the Model DSL just deleted.
37

39	
40	- Full dependent types. Shape labels are metadata, not a type
41	  system; mismatches are runtime errors with rich context, not
42	  compile-time rejection. A future saga can tighten this.
43	- Changes to `DenseArray` row-major storage. Labels live on
44	  `Value::Array` wrappers, not inside the array buffer.

46	  it just learns to propagate and validate labels.

51	
52	Identical to Saga 11:
53	
54	1. TDD: failing test first, then implementation, then refactor.
55	2. Quality gates must all pass before commit:
56	   - `cargo test`
57	   - `cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings`
58	   - `cargo fmt --all` + `cargo fmt --all -- --check`
59	   - `markdown-checker -f "**/*.md"` if docs touched
60	   - `sw-checklist`
61	3. Use `/mw-cp` checkpoint process.
62	4. Push immediately after commit.
63	5. Web UI changes rebuild `pages/` via `scripts/build-pages.sh`.
64

66	
67	- `mlpl_array::Shape` with `dims()` and `rank()` accessors.
68	- `Value::Array` / `Value::Model` / `Value::Str` enum in
69	  `mlpl-eval`. Labels would ride on `Value::Array`.
70	- Structured `EvalError` enum per crate, used everywhere errors
71	  surface (good substrate for shape-mismatch improvements).
72	- `:help`, `:vars`, `:models`, `:fns`, `:wsid`, and `:describe`

82	value type without changing any existing behavior.

89	- `shape(x)` continues to return the raw dim vector. New
90	  `labels(x)` built-in returns a string vector of the axis names

154	  but before "Linear Algebra", so every subsequent lesson can use
155	  labels.
156	- Update the Model DSL lesson and the moons/transformer demos to

158	  report `[seq, d_model]` inputs and outputs on `apply(mdl, X)`.
159	- Update `docs/are-we-driven-yet.md`: move Named Axes,
160	  Shape-Checked Arrays, Structured Errors, and `:describe` from
161	  CONS to PLAN/HAVE.
162	- Update `docs/plan.md` to mark Saga 11.5 COMPLETE.
163	- Bump REPL banners to v0.7.5.
164	- Rebuild and deploy `pages/`.
165	- Tag `v0.7.5-named-axes`.

168	
169	| # | Slug | Phase | What it delivers |
170	|---|------|-------|------------------|
171	| 001 | labeled-shape-type | 1 | `LabeledShape` + `labels()` built-in; no behavior change |
172	| 002 | label-introduction | 2 | `label(x, [...])`, annotation syntax on assignment |
173	| 003 | label-reshape-rules | 2 | transpose preserves, reshape clears, `reshape_labeled` added |
174	| 004 | label-propagation-elementwise | 3 | +, -, *, / propagate and validate labels |
175	| 005 | label-propagation-matmul-reduce | 3 | matmul, reduce_add, softmax by axis name |
176	| 006 | shape-mismatch-error | 4 | Structured `ShapeMismatch` error variant + rendering |
177	| 007 | describe-labels-trace | 5 | `:describe` / `:vars` learn labels; trace JSON includes axis labels |
178	| 008 | named-axes-tutorial-lesson | 6 | New lesson + Model DSL lesson refresh |
179	| 009 | named-axes-release-v075 | 6 | docs, banners, release tag |
180

182	introspection commands (`:describe`, `:vars`, `:models`, `:fns`)
183	already shipped in Saga 11, so phase 5 is now scoped to teach
184	those commands about labels and add labels to the trace export.
185	Expect some merging once implementation starts -- steps 004 and
186	005 in particular may collapse if the elementwise path
187	generalizes cleanly.

189	## Success criteria
190	
191	- A labeled array prints its labels alongside its shape in the
192	  REPL: `X: [seq=6, d_model=4]`.
193	- A deliberately-wrong matmul (e.g. `matmul(A_labeled[batch, dim],
194	  B_labeled[time, dim])`) raises a structured `ShapeMismatch`
195	  error naming the op, the expected contraction axis, and the
196	  actual labels.
197	- `:describe mdl` on a stored model prints its layer tree with
198	  the expected input and output labeled shapes for the first
199	  layer.
200	- `:vars` lists every bound array with its labeled shape.
201	- Every existing demo still runs unchanged: positional arrays
202	  continue to work without labels.
203	- `docs/are-we-driven-yet.md` shows at least four rows moving
204	  from CONS to HAVE.
205	- All quality gates green; pages deployed; release tagged.

208	
209	- **Label propagation through broadcasting.** Scalar broadcast is
210	  easy. Row-vector-against-matrix broadcast is fine if only one
211	  side is labeled. Two labeled sides with compatible dims but
212	  different labels is genuinely ambiguous -- should it error, or
213	  silently prefer the left-hand labels? Default proposal: error,
214	  with an explicit `relabel(x, [...])` escape hatch.
215	- **Parser impact of the annotation syntax.** `x : [a, b, c] = ...`
216	  introduces a colon in assignment that the current parser does
217	  not expect. Step 002 may require a small parser addition; keep
218	  it contained so the rest of the grammar is unaffected.
219	- **`ModelSpec` labeling.** Models are defined before they see any
220	  input, so their input labels are unknown at construction time.
221	  Proposal: track labels opportunistically -- the first `apply`
222	  call pins them, and subsequent `apply` calls with mismatched
223	  labels raise a structured error. Alternative: require models
224	  to be constructed with an explicit signature. Decide in step 005.
225	- **Rank-3+ tensors.** The current op surface is largely rank-2.
226	  Labels for rank-3+ are trivial metadata-wise, but per-head
227	  attention (multi-head, currently blocked on slicing) would
228	  benefit from labeled rank-3 paths. Out of scope for this saga;
229	  note it as a hand-off to a later attention-slicing saga.

- `EvalError::ShapeMismatch { op, expected: LabeledShape, actual: LabeledShape }`
  rendered as a rich REPL message (with colors in the web UI) and
  as a JSON object when an environment flag is set.
- The web REPL's error formatter learns the new variant and shows
  a one-line "expected ... got ... at axis ..." summary with the
  offending op name.
- The existing error site in `mlpl-eval::eval_ops` for broadcasting
  failures migrates to the new variant.

### Phase 5: Label-aware introspection and trace

The REPL introspection commands `:vars`, `:models`, `:fns`,
`:wsid`, and `:describe` already shipped as part of Saga 11. This
phase teaches them about labels and threads labels through the
trace surface:

- `:describe <name>` learns to print a variable's labeled shape
  alongside its raw dims. For models it prints the `ModelSpec`
  tree with per-layer labeled shapes on the input/output, pinned
  from the first `apply` call.
- `:vars` output includes labeled shape for every labeled array.
- `trace` JSON export includes axis labels so downstream tooling
  can reason about shape flow through a run.

### Phase 6: Docs, tutorial, release

- New tutorial lesson "Named Axes" immediately after "Matrices"
  but before "Linear Algebra", so every subsequent lesson can use
  labels.
- Update the Model DSL lesson and the moons/transformer demos to
  label their inputs and outputs. The Model DSL itself should
  report `[seq, d_model]` inputs and outputs on `apply(mdl, X)`.
- Update `docs/are-we-driven-yet.md`: move Named Axes,
  Shape-Checked Arrays, Structured Errors, and `:describe` from
  CONS to PLAN/HAVE.
- Update `docs/plan.md` to mark Saga 11.5 COMPLETE.
- Bump REPL banners to v0.7.5.
- Rebuild and deploy `pages/`.
- Tag `v0.7.5-named-axes`.

## Planned steps

| # | Slug | Phase | What it delivers |
|---|------|-------|------------------|
| 001 | labeled-shape-type | 1 | `LabeledShape` + `labels()` built-in; no behavior change |
| 002 | label-introduction | 2 | `label(x, [...])`, annotation syntax on assignment |
| 003 | label-reshape-rules | 2 | transpose preserves, reshape clears, `reshape_labeled` added |
| 004 | label-propagation-elementwise | 3 | +, -, *, / propagate and validate labels |
| 005 | label-propagation-matmul-reduce | 3 | matmul, reduce_add, softmax by axis name |
| 006 | shape-mismatch-error | 4 | Structured `ShapeMismatch` error variant + rendering |
| 007 | describe-labels-trace | 5 | `:describe` / `:vars` learn labels; trace JSON includes axis labels |
| 008 | named-axes-tutorial-lesson | 6 | New lesson + Model DSL lesson refresh |
| 009 | named-axes-release-v075 | 6 | docs, banners, release tag |

Nine steps. The original plan had ten; step 007's REPL
introspection commands (`:describe`, `:vars`, `:models`, `:fns`)
already shipped in Saga 11, so phase 5 is now scoped to teach
those commands about labels and add labels to the trace export.
Expect some merging once implementation starts -- steps 004 and
005 in particular may collapse if the elementwise path
generalizes cleanly.

## Success criteria

- A labeled array prints its labels alongside its shape in the
  REPL: `X: [seq=6, d_model=4]`.
- A deliberately-wrong matmul (e.g. `matmul(A_labeled[batch, dim],
  B_labeled[time, dim])`) raises a structured `ShapeMismatch`
  error naming the op, the expected contraction axis, and the
  actual labels.
- `:describe mdl` on a stored model prints its layer tree with
  the expected input and output labeled shapes for the first
  layer.
- `:vars` lists every bound array with its labeled shape.
- Every existing demo still runs unchanged: positional arrays
  continue to work without labels.
- `docs/are-we-driven-yet.md` shows at least four rows moving
  from CONS to HAVE.
- All quality gates green; pages deployed; release tagged.

## Risks and open questions

- **Label propagation through broadcasting.** Scalar broadcast is
  easy. Row-vector-against-matrix broadcast is fine if only one
  side is labeled. Two labeled sides with compatible dims but
  different labels is genuinely ambiguous -- should it error, or
  silently prefer the left-hand labels? Default proposal: error,
  with an explicit `relabel(x, [...])` escape hatch.
- **Parser impact of the annotation syntax.** `x : [a, b, c] = ...`
  introduces a colon in assignment that the current parser does
  not expect. Step 002 may require a small parser addition; keep
  it contained so the rest of the grammar is unaffected.
- **`ModelSpec` labeling.** Models are defined before they see any
  input, so their input labels are unknown at construction time.
  Proposal: track labels opportunistically -- the first `apply`
  call pins them, and subsequent `apply` calls with mismatched
  labels raise a structured error. Alternative: require models
  to be constructed with an explicit signature. Decide in step 005.
- **Rank-3+ tensors.** The current op surface is largely rank-2.
  Labels for rank-3+ are trivial metadata-wise, but per-head
  attention (multi-head, currently blocked on slicing) would
  benefit from labeled rank-3 paths. Out of scope for this saga;
  note it as a hand-off to a later attention-slicing saga.
